questions.q: Who is the protagonist of "तेंदुए का इस्माइल" and what is his true identity revealed at the end of the story?
questions.a: The protagonist is the old man (नंगा बूढ़ा नेह) living under the tree, who is revealed to be a poet (कवि) when the Range Officer recognizes him as the author of "वस्ल का इमला" - a famous poem. A wrong answer (e.g., identifying the mother leopard or the Range Officer as protagonist) reveals the student cannot distinguish between catalyst characters and the central consciousness through whom the story's moral conflict unfolds.

questions.q: Why does the old man remain silent throughout most of the officials' debate about cutting down the tree, and what does this silence reveal about his character?
questions.a: His silence reflects helplessness against bureaucratic machinery and a poet's observational nature - he witnesses injustice but lacks institutional power to stop it. This silence breaks only when he acts to save the cub, showing moral courage transcends his apparent powerlessness. A wrong answer (e.g., "he was scared" or "he didn't understand") reveals the student mistakes passive silence for passive character, missing the distinction between structural powerlessness and moral agency.

questions.q: Identify three specific textual moments where the protagonist's actions reveal his core values, and explain what each moment shows about his character.
questions.a: 1) Refusing to leave the tree despite death threat - values principle over survival. 2) Accepting death calmly ("मैं अभी ठहरा हूँ") - shows dignity and fearlessness. 3) Protecting the cub even when ordered to step aside - demonstrates compassion transcending self-preservation. A wrong answer listing generic traits without textual evidence reveals the student cannot ground analysis in the text, a critical board exam skill.

questions.q: Compare the protagonist's response to the bureaucratic system with the responses of the Range Officer (रेंज ऑफिसर) and the DFO (डीएफओ). What does this contrast reveal about the story's central conflict?
questions.a: The protagonist embodies human conscience and artistic integrity - he resists non-violently but firmly. The Range Officer represents mindless rule-following ("आदेश है काटने का"). The DFO represents pragmatic compromise ("हम यहाँ तक कर सकते हैं"). This three-way contrast structures the story's conflict: bureaucracy vs. humanity, with the poet as the moral anchor. A wrong answer treating all three as similar "authority figures" reveals inability to analyze character as thematic device.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "The protagonist's identity as a poet is merely a plot twist; it doesn't fundamentally change our understanding of his actions throughout the story." Defend your position with textual evidence.
questions.a: The statement is false. His poet identity retroactively illuminates his silence (observation), his fearlessness (truth-teller's courage), and his final act (protecting the vulnerable like poetry protects truth). The Range Officer's reaction - "बहुत बड़ा कवि" - and the order to spare the tree because "यह इस्माइल के नीचे का पेड़ है" confirm his identity transforms the situation. A wrong answer agreeing reveals the student treats character revelation as plot device rather than thematic key.

questions.q: Write a 100-word diary entry from the protagonist's perspective on the night before the tree-cutting, capturing his inner conflict between fear for his life and resolve to protect the cub.
questions.a: A strong entry will show: awareness of mortality ("कल ये पेड़ कटेगा, मैं भी"), poetic observation ("चाँदनी में इस्माइल की आँखें"), moral clarity ("कविता सच बचाती है, मैं भी बचाऊँगा"), and acceptance ("डर नहीं, बस दुख है कि व्यवस्था इतनी अंधी है"). A weak entry focusing only on fear or only on heroism reveals the student cannot synthesize the character's complexity - his simultaneous vulnerability and strength.
